1.pericope_label: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim came this word from the Lord, saying, Stand in the court of the Lord’s house, and speak unto all the cities of Judah, which come to worship in the Lord’s house, all the words that I command thee to speak unto them; diminish not a word: if so be they will hearken, and turn every man from his evil way. If ye will not hearken to me, to walk in my law, then will I make this house like Shiloh

schools.summary: Dates the chapter to the very earliest part of the reign on internal evidence, since the invader is nowhere mentioned and the king is friendly with Egypt, and explains the arrangement of the book by the compiler's interest in the conflict with the false prophets; notes the chapter's own heading, rejects a scheme that makes the chapters following three supplements on true and false prophethood, and reports the critics who take the fuller discourse for the text and this for an epitome, finding confirmation in the surprise that met the mention of Shiloh.

Concludes from the displacement that the book was not put together in order but collected, presses the choice of audience, since the people could not enter the house and the priests and false prophets are passed over as past hope while a people led astray may still be restored, and reads the tentative phrase as a common way of speaking rather than any doubt in God, the thing pointed at being an obstinacy hard to heal; closes on the pairing of law and prophets, the prophets devising nothing new but interpreting.
Calls the chapter totally out of its place and reports two scholars who would move it, one before a much later chapter and one much earlier still.

Defends the choice of place and time against any charge of indiscretion, since the court was the one place inside the sworn enemies' jurisdiction, and supplies the reason for the order not to diminish a word: the prophet might have palliated the matter and exchanged an offensive expression for a plausible one, whereas God's ambassadors must keep to their instructions and vary neither to please men nor to save themselves from harm.

debates.question: Where does this chapter belong, and when was it delivered?

positions.view: the preceding prophecy belongs to the fourth year and this to the accession, with the intervening deposition by the king of Egypt
totally out of its place; two scholars would move it, one before a much later chapter and one much earlier still

the very earliest period of the reign, since the invader is nowhere mentioned and the king is friendly with Egypt; the narratives were brought together by a compiler because each turns on the conflict with the false prophets

the chapter has a heading of its own and is closely connected in matter with those following, though not as a scheme of three supplements on true and false prophethood would have it, since Micah was far from a false prophet and Urijah as little wanting in courage as the man who himself hid from this king
the book was not put together in a regular order at all, but the chapters were collected and the volume formed from them

debates.question: Is this the earlier temple sermon, in full or in summary?

positions.view: the critics take the fuller discourse for the text and this for an epitome with its narrative; the surprise and anger that met the mention of Shiloh suggest it was heard now for the first time, which so far confirms them
the prophet spoke more at large but deemed it enough to show in few words what had been committed to him

debates.question: What does the tentative phrase about hearkening imply?

positions.view: not ignorance or conjecture in God but a longsuffering that grants space for repentance and leaves the disregarder without excuse
a common way of speaking; God had no doubt what would follow, and what is pointed at is the people's obstinacy, hard to heal and yet to be tried
purpose: the terrible threat is uttered in order that it may not be realised

outliers.reading: Defends the prophet's discretion in the choice of place and time, since the message might have been delivered in a corner among friends and was instead delivered in the one place within his sworn enemies' jurisdiction, where the worshippers would credit whatever character the priests gave him; and turns the order not to diminish a word into a rule for ministers, who must keep to their instructions and vary neither to please men nor to save themselves from harm.

Finds the priests and the false prophets deliberately passed over while the people are addressed, since none are in so hopeless a case as corrupt priests while a people led astray by them may still be restored; and answers the apparent redundancy of law and prophets by making the prophets its interpreters, so that those who repudiate the daily duty of learning extinguish the grace of the Spirit.

themes: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah came this word from the Lord, saying,

Thus saith the Lord; Stand in the court of the Lord’s house, and speak unto all the cities of Judah, which come to worship in the Lord’s house, all the words that I command thee to speak unto them; diminish not a word:
If so be they will hearken, and turn every man from his evil way, that I may repent me of the evil, which I purpose to do unto them because of the evil of their doings.
And thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord; If ye will not hearken to me, to walk in my law, which I have set before you,
To hearken to the words of my servants the prophets, whom I sent unto you, both rising up early, and sending them, but ye have not hearkened;
Then will I make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.

7.pericope_label: So the priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the Lord. Now when Jeremiah had made an end of speaking, the priests and the prophets and all the people took him, saying, Thou shalt surely die. And all the people were gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the Lord. When the princes of Judah heard these things, they came up and sat down in the entry of the new gate. Then spake the priests and the prophets, This man is worthy to die

schools.summary: Reads the accusers' formula as forensic language, a judgment of death for this man, and the sentence itself with the Hebrew emphasis of reduplication, and explains the appeal to what the bystanders had heard, since the princes reached the temple only after the arrest; reconstructs the princes' movement from the council chamber down through the king's own entry, identifies one of them as the prophet's later protector, and marks the significance of prophets standing among the accusers.

Refuses to credit the crowd's patience, which was the feigned moderation of hypocrites exact in form and negligent of substance and held only because the people stood by, allows the accusers' premise some weight, since a promise of perpetual habitation and a sentence of desolation seem to make God contrary to himself, and answers that the promise was never a licence to sin; turns the princes' arrival into a rebuke and compares the crowd to a sea, calm of itself until a wind rises.

Calls the princes the king's cabinet counsellors and identifies their seat as the place where the body that judged false prophets used to sit, and states as a rule that in the corrupt state of all kingdoms the ecclesiastical officers have always been the greatest enemies of God's ministers.

Allows the crowd the credit of hearing him out while suspecting a hope of finding something worse to charge him with, and exposes the indictment as a misquotation, since the accusers drop both the condition and the divine agent from the threat to leave a flat prediction against the holy place.

debates.question: Why did they let him finish?

positions.view: they dealt more fairly than some persecutors of ministers have done, though perhaps with a bad design, hoping for something worse to lay to his charge
either reverence for a man who was both priest and prophet, or a secret influence that kept them from disturbing him
no credit is due: there was no teachable spirit in them, and what looks like patience is the feigned moderation of hypocrites, who restrained themselves only because the whole people stood by
the use of the divine name, since in his own name the words would have passed

a misquotation: the threat had been conditional and had God for its agent, and the accusers drop both to leave a flat prediction against the holy place, the same charge afterwards laid against Christ and Stephen

the premise that anything alleged against the temple wrongs God, so that the accused is made a cheat who sets God against himself; there is some weight in it, but the promise of a perpetual habitation was never given as a licence to sin
the comparison with the northern sanctuary, over whose fall they had exulted and whose forsaking they had themselves chanted

debates.question: Who were the princes, and how did they come to be there?

positions.view: the nobles of the privy council, or else the great court of seventy
the king's cabinet counsellors, seated where the body that judged false prophets used to sit

they were in council with the king when the report reached them and came down by the king's own entry, a high gate commanding the crowded court; one was in all probability the prophet's later protector, and the princes throughout are less hostile than the priests
sent by the king only to quell a commotion, their absence until then a shameful sign of contempt, since men had come from remote cities for the preaching they had not troubled to attend

outliers.reading: Makes the presence of prophets among the accusers personal to the accused, who had to separate himself from both the orders he belonged to, the one by birth and the other by a special vocation, his bitterest foes being men who claimed to speak in the same name while tuning their voice to the time; and observes that personal rancour mingles with the class feeling of a priesthood appealing to the secular arm against a blasphemer.

Compares the crowd to the sea, calm of itself until a wind rises, easily stirred by whoever will stir it and as easily brought back, and uses the figure to explain how the same people could condemn in the morning and acquit later the same day.

themes: So the priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the Lord.

Now it came to pass, when Jeremiah had made an end of speaking all that the Lord had commanded him to speak unto all the people, that the priests and the prophets and all the people took him, saying, Thou shalt surely die.

Why hast thou prophesied in the name of the Lord, saying, This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be desolate without an inhabitant? And all the people were gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the Lord.
When the princes of Judah heard these things, then they came up from the king’s house unto the house of the Lord, and sat down in the entry of the new gate of the Lord’s house.
Then spake the priests and the prophets unto the princes and to all the people, saying, This man is worthy to die; for he hath prophesied against this city, as ye have heard with your ears.

12.pericope_label: Then spake Jeremiah unto all the princes and to all the people, saying, The Lord sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that ye have heard. Therefore now amend your ways and your doings, and obey the voice of the Lord your God. As for me, behold, I am in your hand: do with me as seemeth good unto you. But know ye for certain, that if ye put me to death, ye shall surely bring innocent blood upon yourselves

schools.summary: Makes the defence the standing answer of every true prophet, that the Lord has spoken and he can but prophesy, and notes what is absent from it, since the man offers no credentials beyond the message and worked no signs or wonders; points out that the apology is simply the sermon repeated, no irreversible doom having been denounced, and finds the later trial coming unbidden to mind at the verdict, with the difference that here the people side with the prophet.

Observes that the plea plainly pleads nothing but the calling and the command, a long discourse having been judged likely to obscure the main point, turns the repetition into a charge of ingratitude, denies that the words about being in their hand can be read strictly, since a man in his enemies' hand is not out of God's, and reads the warning about innocent blood as spreading guilt two ways, upon the killers and against the city that allowed the deed.

Gives the defence in the first person, the commission being God's and the words his own, and adds that the prophet neither sought this painful office nor ran before he was sent, and that they may do with him what they please but will bring innocent blood upon themselves if they slay him.

Presses the acquittal until it accuses the acquitters, since men who own that the prophet spoke in the name of the Lord, and that this Lord is their God, should have amended their ways, preaching being often protected from the malice of others by those who will not submit to its power themselves.

debates.question: What does the prophet's defence consist of?

positions.view: nothing but his calling and the command he had received, a longer discourse having been judged likely to obscure the main point
the standing answer of every true prophet, with no credentials offered beyond the message itself, no signs or wonders having been worked
a first-person plea that the commission is God's and the words his own, and that he neither sought this painful office nor ran before he was sent
a plea made, on an older judgment, with prudence, humility and constancy

debates.question: In what sense was he in their hand?

positions.view: in their power, since they were the court to which the judging of prophets belonged, and he submits
powerless before accusers and judges, with no appeal left but to the Judge of all

not strictly at all, since a man in his enemies' hand is not out of God's and tyrants cannot touch us with a finger unless permission is given; the words are spoken after a human manner and by concession, because providence is hidden
do with me what you please, but if you slay me you bring innocent blood upon yourselves
that court and country found the words neither seditious nor ill-intended, though those who owned that he spoke in the Lord's name should then have amended their ways
the lay rulers favouring a prophet whom priests would have condemned, as at a later trial, save that here the people are on his side too

the reversal came from the company they were in, since a people blinded by the pomp of the priests would not inquire into the cause and went the other way as soon as the princes were present; whence both how mischievous unjust rulers are and how desirable honest ones
the crowd that had sided with the accusers now joined the court in addressing them

outliers.reading: Points out that the whole apology is simply the message repeated: no irreversible doom had been denounced, pardon on repentance had been held out, and the threat was uttered to produce the repentance that would cancel it; and reads the warning about innocent blood as addressed to the lay judges and the people rather than the accusers, on the belief that they at least would shrink from such a deed, the protest being one of constraint rather than a wilful attack on what his countrymen revered.

Reads the preposition in the warning as spreading guilt two ways, upon the killers as perpetrators and against the city for allowing and countenancing the deed, and insists the warning was given not to save the prophet's life but to move them, since he did not fear death and knew his blood would be precious enough to cost the whole city.

themes: Then spake Jeremiah unto all the princes and to all the people, saying, The Lord sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that ye have heard.
Therefore now amend your ways and your doings, and obey the voice of the Lord your God; and the Lord will repent him of the evil that he hath pronounced against you.
As for me, behold, I am in your hand: do with me as seemeth good and meet unto you.

But know ye for certain, that if ye put me to death, ye shall surely bring innocent blood upon yourselves, and upon this city, and upon the inhabitants thereof: for of a truth the Lord hath sent me unto you to speak all these words in your ears.
Then said the princes and all the people unto the priests and to the prophets; This man is not worthy to die: for he hath spoken to us in the name of the Lord our God.

17.pericope_label: Then rose up certain of the elders of the land, and spake to all the assembly of the people, saying, Micah the Morasthite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, saying, Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest. Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him at all to death? did he not fear the Lord, and the Lord repented him of the evil?

schools.summary: Prefers the literal sense of elders over the official, since the speech requires men old enough to carry a tradition of a century before, notes that the word rendered assembly answers to the term for a Greek town's citizen body, supplies the philology and dating of the earlier prophet's name and oracle, and sharpens the precedent into a principle, that here was a case in which a threat did its work and therefore was not fulfilled; marks too the turn to the hostility of the king.

Doubts the placing of the speech, since Scripture does not always keep the order of events, and thinks the elders interposed while the case was still under deliberation; puts their argument against the charge of novelty, defines the fear of the Lord as true conversion in two parts, and turns the date of the earlier oracle into both a difficulty and a comfort, since even the chief exemplar of a godly king could not make the whole people follow him.

Calls the defence fine and the argument perfectly conclusive, guesses that the prophet's later protector made it, observes that the earlier prophet said things as hard and was not put to death because the people saw he was sent of God, and paraphrases the oracle itself, that Zion should be plowed up and the temple's place grow trees as a forest.

debates.question: Who were the elders, and when did they speak?

positions.view: the same as the princes, court men rising as advocates
the word is rather literal than official, or official including the literal, since the speech requires men old enough to carry the tradition of a century before
a fine defence and a perfectly conclusive argument, made perhaps by the man who afterwards protected the prophet
the placing is doubtful, since Scripture does not always keep the order of events; more likely they interposed while the case was still under deliberation and the crowd not yet pacified
that the charge of novelty is false, since God had been wont before this to speak by his prophets against the city and the temple
that a prophet who said things as hard was not put to death, because the people saw he was sent of God
a principle: here was a case in which a threat did its work and therefore was not fulfilled, doing good and not evil
that neither the king nor the great court ever sought that prophet's life, sat in council on it, or so much as arraigned him

debates.question: What was Hezekiah's fear of the Lord?

positions.view: true conversion, the reverence by which a man shows himself submissive because God is at once Father and Sovereign, with repentance in two parts, displeasure with oneself and the desire to form the whole life by the rule of righteousness
no record of the repentance survives, but it is in keeping with the king's known character, and the elders' closing warning answers exactly to a later counsel about being found to fight against God

outliers.reading: Turns the date of the earlier oracle into a difficulty and then a comfort: it might seem strange that under so religious a king, who spared no labour and shunned no danger where religion required it, things stood disordered enough to call for so severe a denunciation, but the lesson is that even the chief exemplar of a godly ruler could not make the whole people follow him, and good men are confirmed by it, since it is a grievous trial to think one's efforts vain and many go backward.

Supplies the philology of the earlier prophet's name, of which the Hebrew here gives the longer interchangeable form, places his birthplace in Philistine territory, dates the cited words near the close of a ministry begun two reigns earlier, and notes that they stand immediately before a promise of restoration in the last days which appears in identical terms in another book; the outcome of the elders' counsel, he adds, is left to be inferred, and evidently left the prophet free to preach on, though probably under something like surveillance.

themes: Then rose up certain of the elders of the land, and spake to all the assembly of the people, saying,

Micah the Morasthite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and spake to all the people of Judah, saying, Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest.

Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him at all to death? did he not fear the Lord, and besought the Lord, and the Lord repented him of the evil which he had pronounced against them? Thus might we procure great evil against our souls.

20.pericope_label: And there was also a man that prophesied in the name of the Lord, Urijah the son of Shemaiah of Kirjathjearim, who prophesied against this city according to all the words of Jeremiah. And when Jehoiakim the king heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but Urijah fled into Egypt, and they fetched him forth, and the king slew him with the sword. Nevertheless the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah

schools.summary: Declines to assign the Urijah narrative to either party, holding that it cannot belong to the elders' argument and that nothing says the accusers alleged it, and reading it instead as the record that the prophet did not stand alone; fills in the politics of the extradition, the king owing his throne to Egypt and the envoy being his father-in-law, calls the dishonoured burial a brutal outrage against Jewish feeling, and traces the protector's family through three generations, closing the narrative on the reason the prophet escaped.

Canvasses both readings of the narrative before assigning it to the prophet's defenders, moved by the common consent of interpreters and by the two examples running on with nothing between; concedes from the flight that even faithful servants are not always courageous enough to despise every danger, makes the recovery a nefarious compact rather than an exercise of power, explains the common graves as a matter of expense, and reads the adversative particle as the measure of the struggle.

Assigns the narrative to enemies of the prophet, notes that the story is recorded nowhere else in Scripture, observes that the process against the one man was finished before the other's case came on, and adds the danger that remained after acquittal, since popular prejudice was not removed by it and the protector was likely obliged to conceal him.

debates.question: Whose speech is the story of Urijah?

positions.view: not the elders continued, since the instance tells against them, but others in the court who sided with the accusers, as two Jewish commentators and an ancient book explain it, though some take it for the defenders arguing that a second such death would add sin to sin
probably the words of others who were enemies to the prophet

the defenders, on the common consent of interpreters and because the two examples run on with nothing between, so the accusers must already have had their turn; the connecting particle may nevertheless be read adversatively

neither: the verses cannot belong to the elders' argument, telling as they do the other way, and nothing says the accusers alleged them; the narrator wished to record that this prophet did not stand alone

debates.question: Why did the second prophet fare differently?

positions.view: either his words were more vehemently denunciatory, or he was less fortunate in finding a personal protector; the princes who defended the one were against the other

the flight shows that even faithful servants of God are not always courageous enough to despise every danger; the fear was not blameless but did not turn him from his course, since he might have pleased the king and dreaded such perfidy more than death
the process against the first being finished, the second was next to be tried for his life, and fled
the narrative closes on the reason, that one man's hand was with him, a man named among those the reforming king had sent to consult the prophetess
by that man's influence, though acquittal did not remove the popular prejudice and he was likely obliged to conceal him, God's genuine ministers having no favour to expect from his enemies
with great and arduous effort, the adversative particle measuring how fiercely the contention raged, hand in Scripture meaning effort
through a family that furnished three generations of patriotism, the father having carried the recovered book of the law to the king and taken this son with him to the prophetess
through one of the old king's counsellors, who used all his power and interest

outliers.reading: Calls the dishonoured burial a brutal outrage by Jewish feeling, the body denied the sepulchre of its fathers and the honour of embalmment and flung into the loathsome pits of the common people, and notes, for those who believe in a special as well as a righteous retribution, that the king who added this brutality to his cruelty was himself afterwards buried with the burial of an ass.

Makes the recovery from Egypt a matter of diplomacy rather than power, since the king complained of a turbulent fugitive and asked for his surrender, so that the man was brought back by a nefarious compact; and explains the common graves as a matter of expense, the rich each having his own while a great number are thrown together, so that a fresh disgrace was prepared for the prophet after death.

themes: And there was also a man that prophesied in the name of the Lord, Urijah the son of Shemaiah of Kirjath–jearim, who prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah:

And when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death: but when Urijah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt;
And Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, namely, Elnathan the son of Achbor, and certain men with him into Egypt.
And they fetched forth Urijah out of Egypt, and brought him unto Jehoiakim the king; who slew him with the sword, and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people.
Nevertheless the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, that they should not give him into the hand of the people to put him to death.
